strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies the gap of unknown exposure mapping functions in peer effect estimation with practical implications
Clever technical design: ego network transformation elegantly addresses GNN expressiveness limitations for capturing closed triads and complex structures
Solid theoretical analysis: Proposition 2 formally establishes expressiveness advantages over standard MPGNNs; clear causal identification framework
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple network models, peer exposure mechanisms, 9 baselines, ablation studies, and robustness tests on noisy networks
Strong empirical results: generally outperforms or matches baselines, with particularly strong performance on structural mechanisms; results improve with edge density as expected
Good reproducibility practices: promise of code release, detailed experimental procedures, clear dataset generation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution (ego network transformation) is relatively straightforward—applying standard GNNs to transformed graphs. Other components (MPGNN features, TARNet outcome models, standard regularization losses) are combinations of existing techniques

Unclear positioning relative to concurrent work: overlaps with Mao et al. (2025), Wu et al. (2025), and Adhikari & Zheleva (2025) on learning exposure functions/embeddings. Differentiation (ego networks vs. off-the-shelf GNNs) is incremental rather than fundamental

Experimental setup concerns: (1) Synthetic outcomes generated using assumed exposure function—may advantage flexible learners; (2) Only 2 real networks, both social (generalization unclear); (3) Limited real-world validation; (4) Some improvements within error margins without significance tests

Scalability not addressed: time complexity is O(ρE × avg(D)) relative to standard GNNs; 5.7s/iteration on 5K nodes; paper acknowledges but relegates to future work with no concrete solutions or large-scale experiments

Design choices lack justification: log transformation (Eq. 7), specific graph readout formula, combination of 5+ hyperparameters chosen via grid search. Table 6 shows sensitivity to λbal; Table 7 to output dimension—insufficient robustness analysis

Theoretical analysis incremental: Proposition 2 is constructive but lacks expressiveness bounds or characterization of limitations. No variance bounds. Error decomposition (A.4.4) identifies terms but provides no tight bounds. Mainly adapts existing results

Strong assumptions with limited analysis: Assumption 2 (immediate neighborhood interference) restrictive for many domains; Assumption 3 (unconfoundedness) untestable with no sensitivity analysis. Table 3 shows even learned exposures have moderate correlations (0.29-0.81) with true functions—identifiability not discussed

Incomplete evaluation: moderate correlation values in Table 3 unexplained; unclear if method learns different but equally valid functions; no performance vs. network size analysis; limited failure case discussion

Presentation issues: Figure 2 dense and hard to parse; 9 content pages before appendix; architectural motivation sometimes unclear (e.g., why concatenate edge attributes instead of attention-based methods)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing misspecified exposure mapping functions in peer effect estimation
Clever insight using ego network transformation to enable closed triad counting, addressing limitations of standard MPGNNs
Solid theoretical analysis establishing expressiveness guarantees (Proposition 2) for causal network motifs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple network models, baselines, and ablation studies supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation with informative figures and extensive documentation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (MLPs, MPGNNs, TARNet/CFR) are standard; ego network transformation feels incremental

Critical experimental limitation: all evaluation uses synthetic/semi-synthetic data with known ground-truth exposure functions for both data generation and evaluation, creating circular validation that doesn't address handling of truly unknown mechanisms

Theory-practice gap: Proposition 2 establishes expressiveness in principle but provides no finite-sample learning guarantees or convergence analysis; connection between theoretical expressiveness and empirical learning performance is assumed not proven

Many unjustified design choices: log transformation (Eq. 7), coverage loss formulation, masked weights architecture, and multiple hyperparameters (λ_cov, λ_ent, λ_sp, λ_bal) lack ablation or principled justification
Scalability concerns: O(N × ρ_E × avg(D)²) complexity with ~5.7 seconds per iteration on moderate-sized networks; no experiments on large-scale graphs

Incomplete empirical analysis: Table 3 validation of learned representations only on single dataset without effect modification; ablation improvements often modest or within error bars; no failure mode analysis

Practical applicability severely limited: restrictive assumptions (neighborhood interference, unconfoundedness), limited guidance on hyperparameter selection, and unclear how method handles exposure functions outside its framework
Problematic evaluation metric: ε_PEHE requires knowing true counterfactual outcomes which requires knowing true exposure function—undermining claims of handling unknown mechanisms

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in causal inference: automatically learning exposure mapping functions when the true function is unknown, which leads to biased effect estimation when misspecified
Clever technical approach using ego network transformation to overcome GNN expressiveness limitations for counting closed triads, enabling standard MPGNNs to capture triangle structures

Rigorous theoretical contributions including Proposition 2 proving EGONETGNN can capture all dyad/open triad/closed triad/open tetrad motifs (whereas standard MPGNNs cannot capture closed triads per Corollary 3.4), plus time complexity and error bound analysis

Exceptionally comprehensive empirical evaluation: 3 synthetic networks (BA, WS, SBM) × 5 underlying mechanisms × 11 baselines + semi-synthetic real networks (BlogCatalog, Flickr), with detailed ablations, sensitivity analyses, and multiple runs with reported standard deviations
Consistent and substantial empirical improvements across all settings, particularly strong for structure-dependent mechanisms (e.g., mutual connections where closed triads matter)

Thoughtfully designed architecture with multiple regularization components (masked weights for invariance, coverage/entropy/sparsity losses for robustness, bounded output) that are well-motivated and shown to contribute through ablations
Strong reproducibility practices: code provided, detailed experimental setup, hyperparameter documentation, multiple runs reported
Clear presentation with good motivating examples, intuitive problem setup, and well-organized technical contributions
weaknesses: Limited real-world validation: Even semi-synthetic experiments (BlogCatalog, Flickr) use synthetically generated outcomes based on assumed mechanisms. No validation on actual peer effect datasets with ground-truth exposure functions, limiting confidence in real-world applicability

Significant computational complexity: Method is ~ρ_E × avg(D) times more expensive than standard MPGNNs, with runtimes of 2.1-5.7 seconds per iteration for 3000-5000 nodes. Scalability to large networks unclear, and no guidance provided on when the computational cost is justified

Identifiability of exposure mapping functions not adequately addressed: While Assumption 3 enables peer effect identification, multiple exposure mappings could yield identical outcome distributions. No discussion of when φ_e is uniquely identifiable

Strong untestable assumptions including Neighborhood Interference (immediate neighbors only) and Unconfoundedness (all confounders observed), which are standard but limit practical applicability. Pre-treatment network assumption may not hold when network is influenced by treatments

Theory-practice gap: Proposition 2 proves EGONETGNN can capture motifs but provides no guarantees the model will learn the true function. No sample complexity bounds or convergence analysis. Sequential error decomposition (A.4.4) is loose. Authors acknowledge missing variance bounds

Limited interpretability analysis: Table 3 shows correlation with true exposure but offers minimal insight into what exposure functions are actually learned. No investigation of whether learned representations are stable, interpretable, or comparable to manual motif-based approaches

Experimental design questions: (1) Model selection based on outcome prediction loss rather than peer effect estimation error may favor outcome model; (2) Extensive hyperparameter tuning for proposed method vs. defaults for most baselines may overstate improvements; (3) Baselines mostly use untuned off-the-shelf GNNs rather than architecturally similar comparisons

Incomplete guidance for practitioners: Paper does not discuss when expensive EGONETGNN is necessary versus simpler methods. For many settings, baselines are competitive, suggesting simpler approaches may suffice in practice

Missing analyses: No ablation on individual loss components (coverage vs. entropy vs. sparsity), limited justification for graph readout design choices, no comparison with grid search over hand-crafted exposure functions baseline
Notation becomes dense in places, Figure 2 is complex to parse, and some key design choices (e.g., X̄_j = Z_ij for edge-to-node transformation) lack sufficient justification
